Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:1: Since we were occupied, in the previous chapter, with the necessity of fasting for the penitent, in order to humble his heart, and we spoke of the things needed on the day of the fast, we said we would explain, in a chapter of its own, further things needed for the fast, and the things the penitent should contemplate so that he fast with a good heart and a willing soul, and weep from heart and soul over his iniquities, to fulfill the verse (Joel 2:12), "with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning" - for when the penitent contemplates what we explained in the Gate of Fear (chapter 9) concerning the reality of iniquity, how much evil it causes him, his soul, and the whole world, and that the matter of the blemish touches even the supernal worlds, certainly he will regret with complete regret all his iniquities, and see with the eye of his intellect how many deeds he must do to appease the Master of all, whom he angered with his evil deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:2: And let him consider: had he sinned against a king of flesh and blood, and owed his head to the king, how much would he need to do to appease him! And if they told him, fast so many fasts and give from your money such and such, he would give everything he owns for his life, as it is written (Job 2:4), "skin for skin, and all that a man has will he give for his life." All the more so, by an a fortiori argument, one who has sinned before the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and owes his head to the King - and whoever says the Holy One, blessed be He, is lenient, his own intestines shall be treated leniently [i.e., he shall be judged harshly] (Bava Kamma 50b; Yerushalmi Beitzah, chapter 3, halachah 8) - rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, is patient and collects His due (cf. Yerushalmi ibid.) - so one must appease his Owner with whatever will reconcile Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:3: And they explained in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 202a), in these words: come and see, for how many generations does the Holy One, blessed be He, collect payment for the iniquities of the tribes! For nothing is lost before the Holy One, blessed be He, and He collects from generation to generation, and judgment stands before Him always until He collects and the judgment rests where it is needed. From where do we learn this? From Chizkiyahu, and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:4: And in Sefer Chassidim (section 344) he wrote a good parable for this matter, in these words: see how many fasts, fasting, weeping, and supplications a person performs when his son is ill, for his soul is bitter over his son - all the more so should he do this when he commits a transgression, which destroys the good of his soul forever - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:5: Further, let him consider another parable: if he had a great wound spreading through his whole limb, until the doctors say, if the wound spreads and reaches the heart, he will die - and then they are commanded to cut off that limb in order to save the other limbs, whose life depends on the heart. And behold, without doubt the patient is then in great distress, crying out, woe, woe, and no one has mercy on him - yet whatever they do to him in the matter of healing, cutting the diseased flesh and applying bandages, even though they are painful, is all mercy and kindness to him, to save his soul. So the penitent should liken this very same thing to the matter of self-affliction, and see that it is necessary for him in order to finish off the filth of his inclination and subdue it, and to bring his soul to the good path - so that even though he suffers, he should accept that suffering with a joyful countenance, and not rebel against the suffering, as the liturgical poet said, "he shall bear the yoke and not wither," and shall not be disgusted by reproof - for if he fasts one day and suffers, he should not wither and cast off the burden of repentance from himself, saying, what have I to do with this distress? Better for me to eat and drink - as it is said (Jeremiah 22:15), "did not your father eat and drink," and so on - "then it was well with him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:6: For certainly one who has not sinned has no need for fasting and self-affliction, but one who has sinned needs it, as we explained above in chapter 3, and the greatest proof is from King David, peace be upon him. Especially one who is afflicted with the leprosy of his iniquities, "from the sole of his foot to his crown there is no soundness in him" - a month or months will not suffice to finish off his impurity from him; would that all his days suffice to purify his iniquities, and that they all be clean from now on, without further iniquity.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:7: For a sinner who sins once leaves a mark, and that mark needs washing - and if, before washing, he sins again and repeats it, that mark becomes stronger still; and if a third time, the mark spreads from one side to the other, and it is harder to purify - as this matter is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Noach, page 73b), in these words: he opened and said (Psalms 51:5), "for I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is always before me" - how much people must guard themselves from their sins before the Holy One, blessed be He! For once a person sins, his sin is marked above, and it is not erased except through the strength of great repentance, along the lines of (Jeremiah 2:22), "for though you wash yourself with lye, and use much soap, yet your iniquity is marked before Me." Come and see, once a person sins before the Holy One, blessed be He, one time, it makes a mark; and when he sins a second time, that mark strengthens further; if he sins a third time, that stain spreads from this side to that side - then it is written, "your iniquity is marked before Me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:8: Come and see King David - once David sinned before the Holy One, blessed be He, in the matter of Bathsheba, he thought that sin was marked upon him forever. What is written (2 Samuel 12:13)? "The LORD also has removed your sin; you shall not die" - He removed that mark from before Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:9: And he further says on: come and see, David, even though he confessed his sin and returned in repentance, his heart and his will did not depart from those sins he sinned, and from that sin of Bathsheba, because he always feared them, lest one of them cause harm and accuse him at a time of danger - and therefore they were never forgotten by him or from his will - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:10: And the words of this discourse should inflame the penitent's heart to perform proper repentance - for it says that when a person sins once, his iniquity is marked and written, as the prophet said (Jeremiah 17:1), "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron," and so on, and in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 223b) they explained the matter of the "pen of iron" and "the point of a diamond," in these words: its point - all those [angels] who mention people's sins and write and mark their sins with the strength of harsh judgment - and therefore it is written, "the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with the point of a diamond" - what is "diamond"? That which pierces stone and penetrates it on every side - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:11: And iniquity is erased only through the power of strong repentance, along the lines of (Jeremiah 2:22), "for though you wash yourself with lye, and use much soap" - and it is known that "lye" and "soap" for iniquity is purification through self-affliction, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, as King David, peace be upon him, did for one iniquity - and if for one iniquity strong repentance is needed, more than lye and soap, one whose whole life was in darkness - how much more lye and soap does he need, until his soul whitens from the darkness and the great blemish that darkened it!
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:12: For as sin enters little by little into the husk, until the whole stature of his soul is clothed in the husk, then it is said (Ezra 9:6), "for our iniquities have increased over our head" - and this is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 38:5), "there is no soundness in my flesh because of Your indignation; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin; for my iniquities have gone over my head; as a heavy burden they are too heavy for me" - and he also said (ibid. 69:3), "I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing; I have come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:13: And concerning this the penitent shall be embittered, to fast, weep, and pray, and say to his soul: my soul, how did I put you to death with my own hands? Dear daughter, how did I uproot you from the place of life and holiness to the place of death and impurity? How did I not have compassion on you? And let him consider: if a person unwittingly killed his beloved only son, and it later became known to him, or intentionally and he regretted it - is it not fitting that he be embittered and weep over him, as Jacob our father, peace be upon him, did over Joseph, putting on sackcloth and mourning over him many days (Genesis 37:34), which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Bereshit Rabbah 84:20), as twenty-two years, until he was informed about Joseph - and if they told him, do such and such and you will revive him, he would certainly do it. So it is fitting to be embittered and weep over what has passed, and to be in mourning all his days over having killed his own precious soul - and especially if he has the iniquity of emitting seed in vain, for he has killed his own children, certainly deserving of great mourning - and he should strive to return, pray, and cast off from himself all his transgressions, and to be careful and alert in divine service, in order to revive his soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:14: And when he further considers what was explained in the Gate of Fear (chapters 7, 8), that iniquity is a wound in the soul, he shall be embittered when he considers how many sword-wounds have struck his soul and killed it. And let him imagine: if he had several sword-wounds, and was blind in his eyes, and his hands maimed, and his legs lame, and the rest of his body full of wounds and bruises, how much would it be fitting for him to weep! So let him weep over the wounds in his soul - for he is blind in his eyes, not seeing what is fitting to see, and his ears do not hear what is fitting to hear - and correspondingly they said (Berachot 18b), the wicked, in their lifetime, are called dead, for the soul within them is as though dead, and no spiritual actions are performed by their body - and this is what they said in the Zohar several times: woe to the people whose hearts are sealed, whose eyes are closed, whose ears are stopped, and the like. It follows that the iniquities marked in the soul are wounds and plagues, requiring healing - and concerning this King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 41:5), "I said, LORD, be gracious to me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against You" - and it is good to intend this in the blessing "heal us," concerning the illnesses of the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:15: Further, a person shall weep when he considers his death, and how his soul will appear above, before the holy ones, with so many defects, and how much shame and disgrace shall reach him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:16: And the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, wrote, on the mishnah (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 1), "and all your deeds are written in a book," in these words: he said, behold I am like one seventy years old; "the days of our years are seventy years" - they are already forgotten. It is not so, for your deeds are written in a book - and what is this book? A person's own soul, as he says, who testifies against him? His own soul, as it is said (Micah 7:5), "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom" - for in the soul the commandments and transgressions are engraved. To what may this be compared? To a person full of plagues in his body, but his garment covers them - and when his garment is removed, his nakedness is revealed and his disgrace seen. So too, while the soul is clothed in matter, as it is said (Job 33:17), "and he covers the pride of man" - the defects of transgression are not seen; but when the matter is removed from the soul, its nakedness is revealed and its disgrace seen - woe to that shame! And this is what is said (ibid. 37:7), "He seals up the hand of every man, that all men may know his work" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:17: Also, let him intend, by weeping, to erase the accusations that accuse him - for one who commits a single transgression acquires a single accuser (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 11) - and when he pictures his soul's ascent above, and how many accusers accuse it and push it outside, it is fitting that he weep, mourn, and be ashamed of his sins - and through tears his accusers are nullified, as the liturgical poet said, "I pour out my tears to You, wipe away my sins with my tears."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:18: And therefore it is fitting to pass the tear over his forehead and his face, where the iniquities are marked - and in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b) they explained that Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosi were walking on the road, and saw a man whose face was marked, and they said, this is a sinner - and they said, at the end of the account, he said to them, who is your healer? He said to them, Rabbi Simlai. He said to them, what remedy did he give you? He said to them, the remedy of the soul, and from that day I returned in repentance, and every day I look at my face on the side of a mirror, and I weep before the Holy One, blessed be He, who is Master of the universe, over that sin, and with those tears I wash my face - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:19: And he should intend to wash the blemish and darkness in the face through the water flowing from his eyes, just as the supernal blemish is washed through the waters of the supernal river, as explained in the Idra of Naso, in the repairs of the supernal beard, in the second repair (page 132b), where he says: and one that was dark, was washed in that light, like one washed in that deep river - and he further says, what is the resolution of what you have seen? They opened and said, "who forgives iniquity" you have seen - to this point. It follows that iniquity is darkness, and it is whitened through the supernal light; so too below, in man, the darkness within him is washed through the water descending from his eyes, for the gates of tears are never locked - and so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 223a): and come and see, we have learned, that righteous woman Leah shed abundant tears, in order to be Jacob's portion and not that wicked Esau's - and this is what we have learned: any person who sheds tears before the Holy One, blessed be He, even though a punishment was decreed against him, it is torn up, and that punishment cannot rule over him - from where do we learn this? From Leah - for Leah was decreed to be Esau's portion, and she preceded him with supplication for Jacob, and was not given to Esau - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:20: And it appears to me that through this may be understood the verse (Psalms 6:9), "depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping" - and "the workers of iniquity" are the external accusers, who depart through weeping.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:21: Further, in the Zohar (Parashat Shemot, page 12b), Rabbi Yehuda said: all matters in the world depend on repentance and on the prayer a person prays to the Holy One, blessed be He - and all the more so one who sheds tears in his prayer, for there is no gate that those tears do not enter. What is written (Exodus 2:6)? "And she opened it, and saw the child; and behold, the boy wept" - "and she opened it" - this is the Shechinah, who stands over Israel like a mother over her children, and she always opens on Israel's behalf. Once she opened and saw the child - a beloved child, namely Israel, who sin before their Master in everything, and immediately return in repentance and weep before Him like a son weeping before his father - what is written? "And behold, the boy wept" - once he weeps, all harsh, evil decrees are broken. What is written? "And she had compassion on him" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:22: And so in the Tikkunim (Tikkun 11, page 26b), he says: when Israel would pray, all the chambers would open toward them - but now, in exile, it is said of them, "all the gates are locked," for the Shechinah is outside her chambers, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is outside His chambers, and the angels appointed over prayers are outside their chambers - this is what is written (Psalms 51:17), "O Lord, open my lips" - with what shall I open it? With tears - this is what is written, "and behold, the boy wept," immediately, "and she had compassion on him." And further, "and she opened" - when Israel open in repentance with weeping, immediately "she had compassion on him" - certainly "with weeping shall they come" (Jeremiah 31:8) - in the merit of his weeping they shall be gathered from exile. "Bechi" [weeping] equals "Bnei Yisrael" [numerically] - a tear is "bat ayin" [daughter of the eye], a small yud, for there is a chamber of tears that has no permission to open except through tears - to this point. And at the end of the Tikkun he says, there is no gate open except that of tears - and what is it? "Bat ayin" [pupil of the eye], from which the tear emerges, and of it is said (Psalms 17:8), "keep me as the apple [ishon, lit. "little man"] of the eye [bat ayin]" - to this point. And as he weeps, let him confess the confession written in Sefer Chassidim (section 171).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:23: And concerning the order of the fasts and repentance, how one should do it, it is written in Sefer HaKanah, in these words: and I say to you, my son: whoever wishes to return in repentance should despair of this world, and not engage in business or trade of any kind in this world, and should think in his heart that at every hour the King will come to him to take a reckoning of his iniquities, and shall not eat meat nor anything that has the breath of life in its nostrils, nor drink wine, and shall sit in a fast and occupy himself with Torah day and night, and wage war against sleep, so as not to be forced to sleep the whole night, and draw all his thought to the LORD, blessed be He, and regret everything he has done; and if a transgression comes into his hand, let him push it away and distance it from himself; and his essential food should be bread by weight, enough for his sustenance. And he should do this: he should distance himself from worldly company, from eating meat and wine, from any living creature, from things that come from a living creature, and from all kinds of vegetables, and do this for forty days - and from there on the Holy One, blessed be He, will help him, and he shall continue until six years, and then he need not have any doubt that he is a son of the World to Come, even if he eats after six years, since six years have already passed over him, corresponding to the six thousand years the world exists and one destroyed - provided that from then on he is careful of the transgressions that come into his hand.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:24: He said to me, my son, this is the true, excellent repentance - for the Holy One, blessed be He, loves that man be humbled and lowered before Him, and remember the day of death when he comes in and goes out, when he lies down and rises up, and when he walks on the road - and this is impossible with eating, drinking, and fine garments, for the Torah says (Deuteronomy 32:15), "but Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:25: And know, my son, that eating and drinking are all external matters, and they are good for the emanated ones from outside, who are the deniers - but the holy, inward Israel, all their eating must be in holiness, purity, and great precision. And so too, all marital relations are drawn after the inclination, and are good for those who come from the side of the inclination - but Israel, pure and clean, when he comes to his wife, his intention shall be for the commandments of his God, and he shall seek from the Name a pure, clean soul - and then the Name sees that his intention is for good, and emanates for him a precious, pure soul, and grants merit to him and to the whole world. And this intention does not come from the side of eating, drinking, and fine garments, but only from great humbling.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:26: And see, my son, what I did: I contemplated in my heart to perform repentance, and I did not know [how] - and I sat in a fast for one hundred and twenty days on scant bread, and nothing came into my mouth all those days except bread soaked in a very small amount of water, and every day I poured out my soul in prayer to the LORD and in my study - and at the end of one hundred and twenty days Elijah, of blessed memory, came and said to me: do not suffer any more, my son, for the Holy One, blessed be He, has accepted your repentance; nevertheless, continue yourself until six years, for the dwelling place of the God of Abraham is your help - and so I did, and I did not feel, all those years, how they passed over me, and truly, from then on, no sin or iniquity came into my hands, for the LORD guarded me, and turning from evil is understanding - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:27: Concerning this reality of self-affliction, we find that Rabbi Yishmael, the High Priest, did so - Rabbi Yishmael, the High Priest, said: I was thirteen years old when I went to Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah, and I asked him, the prince of the Torah - who is he, and what is his name? He said to me, his name is Yofiel - and immediately I stood and added suffering upon suffering, for I was in a fast, and I separated myself from every pleasure for forty days in addition to my fast, and I recited that great Name at the end of forty days until I brought him down, and he descended like a flame of fire, and his face like the appearance of lightning - and when I saw him I was terrified and trembled, and all my limbs came apart, and I fell backward. And he said to me, son of man, what is your nature, that you have startled a great retinue? And I strengthened myself and said to him, it is revealed and known before Him who spoke and the world came into being, that I did not bring you down for my own honor, but to do the will of your Owner. And immediately he said to me, son of man, a putrid drop, a worm and a maggot - even more so is your soul, since it has the company of a wounded body - if so, if you wish that he be revealed to you, sit forty days in a fast and immerse twenty-four immersions each day, and taste nothing defiling, nor any kind of legume or vegetable, and do not gaze upon a woman, and sit in a dark room - and do so, and teach him the Name, and teach - and he would ascend and descend.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:28: And although the pious and holy one, peace be upon him, HaKanah, went to great lengths in the order of repentance, not every person can fulfill it - especially a pampered person, who has grown up all his days in pleasure - if he uproots himself all at once to perform such self-affliction, it is possible he will fall ill; therefore he must conduct himself little by little in the ways of repentance - such as beginning to separate himself from meat and wine, which is called "affliction" [inui], as we find Daniel, peace be upon him, did, as it is said (Daniel 10:3), "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came meat nor wine into my mouth, nor did I anoint myself" - and they said in Tractate Yoma (76b) on this verse: from where do we learn that anointing is called "affliction"? For it is written, "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came meat nor wine into my mouth, nor did I anoint myself" - what is "I ate no pleasant bread"? Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Sheilat said in the name of Rav, he did not eat warm bread of fine wheat. From where do we learn that this is considered "affliction"? For it is written (Daniel 10:12), "and he said, do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself," and so on, "your words were heard, and I have come because of your words, for you are precious" - to this point. And Rashi explained "fine wheat" as beautiful, clean wheat, as we translate "the choice garments" [begadim ha-chamudot] - "clean" - to this point. Behold, all these things mentioned in the verse are considered some degree of "affliction," and anointing, since he did not anoint at all, is the greatest affliction of all - for if you do not say that "affliction" applies only to anointing alone, why is it mentioned in the verse? And further, why did the Gemara need to explain what "pleasant bread" is? Rather, certainly it is to teach us that affliction from pleasant bread is also called "affliction." And along this path, one who is not accustomed to affliction should begin, until he becomes accustomed to subduing his inclination little by little.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:29: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Midrash Yelamdenu, on (Ezekiel 36:26), "and I will remove the stony heart from your flesh" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: remove the evil inclination little by little, as it is said (Isaiah 62:10), "cast up, cast up the highway; gather out the stones" - and in the World to Come I shall uproot it, as it is said, "and I will remove the stony heart from your flesh" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:30: And so the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (end of the Gate of Love), in these words: proceed slowly and gradually in acquiring good attributes, as your circumstances can bear, and beware of excess and going too far without gradation, lest you be lost - for too much oil in a lamp is the cause of extinguishing its light; and beware of neglect, laziness, and slackness, and cleave to alacrity with alacrity - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:31: And everything a person does to accept suffering to afflict his soul shall be counted for him as repentance - for behold, Ahab, who was accustomed to eat at the third hour, ate at the seventh, and so on, as we copied the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in chapter 3. And this is a gradation for acquiring the fast - for he shifts himself from eating at the hour he was accustomed to, until, when he fasts, it will not be hard for him; and afterward he shall accustom himself to fast one day a week, until he becomes accustomed on Monday and Thursday, and afterward accustom himself to a third day, until he becomes accustomed to fasting the whole week and it is not hard, for habit rules over everything, and it becomes nature.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:32: And he shall accustom himself to fast one day with its night - for they said in Tanna D'Vei Eliyahu (Zuta, chapter 4) that Israel fasted forty days, and on the last day they stayed the night in the fast, and it was established as the fast of the Day of Atonement, in which we cease [eating] while it is still day - in these words, in Parashat Ki Tisa: forty days Moses ascended to the heights to bring the Torah to Israel, all those days they observed fasting; and on the last day of all they decreed a fast and stayed the night in the fast - and it concludes further on that that day was established as an atonement for Israel until the end of all generations.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:33: And when he has become accustomed to breaking off the day and its night, let him accustom himself to fast two days and two nights - for the later authorities wrote that these are like forty days without being consecutive, but I have received that they are like twenty-seven consecutive [ordinary days of fasting equal in cumulative merit] - and a person shall accustom himself to all this by shifting himself from eating at the hour he was accustomed, delaying past the usual hour by two or three hours even on a day he fasted, so that he not feel the break on the second night - until he becomes accustomed to the repentance the pious HaKanah, peace be upon him, wrote of, until his repentance ascends to the Throne of Glory, where the World to Come is - and the World to Come has neither eating nor drinking, and since he holds fast to repentance, which is in the World to Come, he must grasp its attributes, which are separation from the matters of this world - from eating, drinking, anointing, and other pleasures. And for this reason the Day of Atonement is forbidden in five afflictions, corresponding to the supernal heh, which is the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:34: And so we find in the first chapter of Ta'anit (chapter 1, mishnah 6), that when three fasts were decreed on the community and they were not answered, three other fasts are decreed, which are forbidden in eating, drinking, washing, anointing, and so on, like the fast of the Day of Atonement - to teach that the complete repentance to ascend to the World to Come is these mentioned. And if an individual wishes to observe one day a week for atonement of his iniquities in this manner, happy is he.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:35: And so the prophet taught us that the levels of repentance to ascend up to the Throne of Glory are these mentioned in the verse (Joel 2:12), "and return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping," and so on - and it says "to Me" [adai], along the lines of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, expounded (Yoma 86a) on "return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" (Hosea 14:2) - great is repentance, for it reaches up to the Throne of Glory.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:36: And I heard in the name of our teacher Rabbi Isaac Luria Ashkenazi, peace be upon him, that the word "teshuvah" [repentance] alludes to the matter of the levels required for it, being an acronym for "*ta'anit" [fast], "*sak" [sackcloth], "*va-efer" [and ashes], "*bechiyah" [weeping], "*hesped" [mourning/eulogy]. And although sackcloth is not mentioned in this verse, it is because it is mentioned in the Torah through Jacob and the Prophets, as we explained above. And it is possible that it is included in "hesped" [mourning], for one who eulogizes his deceased mourns and wears sackcloth and ashes, as Jacob our father, peace be upon him, did - and so it is mentioned in the Scroll of Esther (4:3), "and in every province, wherever the king's command and his decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and mourning; and many lay in sackcloth and ashes."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:37: And one who is ill and cannot fulfill all of them, and fulfills some of them, is still called repentance - and the proof is King Chizkiyahu, peace be upon him, of whom what is mentioned (2 Kings 20:2-3 [sic]) is weeping and prayer, not fasting and sackcloth, because he was ill, and he was answered in his prayer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:38: And one of the things the penitent must do is pray over his iniquities to the Holy One, blessed be He, that He forgive him - and so it is explained in Midrash Tehillim, in the psalm "when he came to her" [Bathsheba], in these words: from here you learn that whoever knows he has sinned, and prays over the sin and fears it, and deliberates between himself and the Omnipresent - the Holy One, blessed be He, forgives him. And whoever knows he has sinned and tramples it underfoot and removes it from before his eyes - the Holy One, blessed be He, seeks it from him [holds him accountable] - and so it says (Psalms 49:6), "why should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me?" - those who extinguish [awareness of the sin] at their heels [trample it], and so on - so anyone who removes his iniquity from before his eyes, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not forgive him; and therefore David said (ibid. 51:5), "and my sin is always before me" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:39: And in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 243b), on the verse "Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path" (Genesis 49:17), in these words: Rabbi Yitzchak said, Dan is the serpent, lurking on the roads and paths - and should you say this refers to Samson, so too, above, this is the small serpent, who gathers all the camps, lurking on the roads and paths, then the hosts and camps, and from here emerge those who lurk for people over the sins they have thrown behind their backs - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 5:40: Also, it is a positive commandment for the penitent to confess his iniquity, as it is said (Numbers 5:7), "then they shall confess their sin which they have done." And the order of confession is "I have sinned, I have committed iniquity, I have transgressed" - and their secret is explained in Parashat Vayikra (Zohar, page 20a), on the verse "against You, You only, have I sinned." And it is customary to confess in alphabetical order, because through the twenty-two letters all the worlds were created, as explained in Sefer Yetzirah, and through iniquity all the worlds are blemished - and therefore it is fitting to confess in alphabetical order.
